name: Ironpass Dock & Freight Handler's Full Kit
description:
A battered but solid head-to-toe kit assembled around the realities of moving heavy cargo on M88's lakefront docks in all weather. The outer layer is a burnt-orange high-visibility vest, the heavy-duty kind with wide reflective silver X-straps across the chest and back, worn over a thick charcoal flannel-lined synth-canvas work shirt with rolled cuffs and a worn Meridian Harbor Authority patch on the left shoulder — the kind of patch that's been heat-pressed, peeled, and re-pressed three times. The shirt has a split back seam with hook-and-eye closure that accommodates a low spinal rig or exo-harness attachment point. Beneath is a plain white thermal undershirt, visible at the neck, collar open. Trousers are heavy-duty navy cargo work pants with reinforced knees, a gusseted crotch for full movement, and exterior thigh pockets with zip and velcro closures — one holding a folded work order tablet sleeve, the other a wedge of reflective tape strips used for on-the-fly equipment marking.

The worker wears a yellow hard hat with a cracked brim repaired with silver adhesive tape, a name written in permanent marker on the back: VADUVA-OSEI. Safety glasses hang from the vest's front pocket D-ring. Hands are covered by thick orange leather grip gloves with reinforced palm pads, knuckles worn pale. Boots are heavy lace-up black rubber-over-leather dock boots with a pronounced ankle guard, rated for chemical splash and equipped with a magnetic-latch safety toe. The whole kit smells faintly of hydraulic fluid and lake water. It's functional, unglamorous, and completely honest.
functionality: Split back seam with hook-and-eye for spinal rig or exo-harness attachment; high-vis vest for crane and heavy equipment zones; reinforced knee and crotch for physical labor range of motion; chemical-splash rated boots with safety toe; D-ring vest attachment for tools and glasses; thigh pockets for work order storage
what_it_says: This is dock labor — essential, physical, and underpaid relative to the cargo value they move. The layered, well-worn state of the kit says this worker has been at it for years, not months. The name marker on the hard hat is a Circuit tradition: you own your gear even when the corponation owns your hours. There's dignity here, but it's self-made.
manufacturer: Meridian Harbor Authority (vest and hard hat issued); work shirt and trousers self-purchased from Ironpass Workwear (street-distributed Circuit brand)
price_range: Φ140–Φ210 (assembled kit; issued pieces replace at Φ40–Φ60 each)
story_hooks: A dock worker's kit is found floating in the harbor, work order tablet still in the thigh pocket — the last logged entry is a cargo manifest that doesn't match any ship in the harbor authority database.

Someone is selling counterfeit Meridian Harbor Authority patches at Circuit market stalls, giving Shelf residents access to restricted dock zones — and someone with this kit is the unwitting face of the operation.

A character wearing this uniform realizes mid-shift that the exo-harness attachment point on their shirt has been tampered with — the hook-and-eye release has been weakened, and they're about to operate heavy machinery twenty meters above the water.
